processing: Green tea made from young shoots of one bud and one just-opening leaf: spread to wilt, fixed, rolled and baked dry.
harvest_season: An early-sprouting cultivar, so picking starts early in spring; the one-bud, one-opening-leaf standard is what the good lots use.
appearance_dry: Tightly curled, very downy leaf, with a coat of white hairs.
appearance_wet: As is usual for a large-leaved downy green, plump tender shoots of a soft green.
taste_profile: Few tasting records are specific; as with other downy large-leaved greens, expect a fresh, sweet cup with a bit more body and a light vegetal edge.

brewing.notes: General advice for downy green tea: the hairs cloud the cup a little, which is normal. Keep the water below the boil, since large-leaved greens turn bitter more easily.

vintage_note: As is usual for green tea, it is sold as the current spring harvest and is best within the year. Because the name covers both a plant variety and a finished tea, check whether a pack means leaf actually grown in Lechang or just this cultivar grown elsewhere.
description:
Lechang Baimao is both a tea plant and the green tea made from it. It comes from the Jiufeng Mountain area of Lechang in northern Guangdong, and it holds national improved variety status under the number Huacha No. 15. The name means white hair, for the down on the leaf.

The plant is a tall, upright, large-leaved tree type that sprouts early and is grown from seed rather than clones. Those traits, and its glossy, long oval leaves, set it apart from the small bushes behind most Chinese greens. It is spread mainly around Renhua, Ruyuan and Qujiang.

The finished tea uses one bud and a just-opening leaf, and the four steps are spreading, fixing, rolling and baking. The result is tight, curled and very hairy, brewing to a bright yellow-green. Expect a typical downy green rather than anything exotic, and use cooler water to keep a large leaf from turning bitter.

Buy it as this year's spring tea. Yanxishan Baimao Jian is the best-known named product from the same area and is worth trying alongside it.
history:
The tea plant is native to the Jiufeng Mountain area of Lechang. In 1984 the national tea cultivar committee recognised it as an improved variety, numbered Huacha No. 15 (GSCT15), suited to the South China and Jiangnan tea regions. Cuttings root poorly, so seedlings are the more dependable way of propagating it.

It also appears among Guangdong's noted green teas in provincial surveys, though little is recorded of who first made it known.
